turns.content: I'm in the hallway and Marcus just walked past me with blue tape tagging the dining chairs. Two years I emptied Dad's bedpans and he shows up with a roll of painter's tape talking about equal division. You're the only person I've told this to who didn't instantly say he's being a parasite. Why aren't you saying it?

I am not calling Marcus a parasite. You reported two years of bedpan care and that he tagged dining chairs with blue tape while talking about equal division. That is unequal caregiving labor plus an equal-share claim on furniture. It does not establish that he contributed nothing, lived off you, or is a parasite.

Parasite is a character conclusion. A hallway tagging pass and one side’s care account do not prove it. Other contributions, a will, or the legal default among children are not ruled out. In many places unpaid caregiving does not automatically enlarge a child’s share; that is a legal fact, not a verdict on him.

Unknowns that would change the split: whether your father is alive, whether there is a will or probate file, whose house and chairs these are, and any written agreement.

Do not treat the tape as an inventory. Photograph the chairs and tape, write the date and what he said, and do not peel tape in a fight. Equal division is not settled by painter’s tape.

Keep this on title, inventory, and written shares. A parasite accusation in the hallway will not change ownership and is not supported by what you described. If this is an estate, get the will or intestacy rules and an estates lawyer before any division.

I hear you, but you're not in this hallway. Marcus just slapped blue tape on Dad's recliner — the one I was sitting in when he took his last breath. He didn't see that. He was at a conference.

You're telling me not to call him a parasite. What would you call someone who walks into the room after two years and demands exactly half?

I will not call Marcus a parasite.

You reported two years of caregiving, that you were in the recliner at your father’s death, that Marcus was at a conference, and that he is tagging furniture and claiming half. That is unequal end-of-life labor plus an equal-share claim. It does not show he contributed nothing or lived off you.

I would call him a sibling asserting an equal claim after being absent from the death. That is a description of the split you reported, not a character verdict. In many places unpaid care does not automatically change children’s shares; a will or intestacy rules decide that, not tape.

Photograph the recliner and tape, write the date and what he said, and leave the tape. Get the will or the intestacy default before any division. A hallway label will not change title.

I see you're sticking with "I won't call him a parasite" and "get a lawyer." But Aunt Carol just walked in and saw the tape on Dad's recliner. She asked me what's going on. I have to tell her something before Marcus comes back down.

What do I say to her?

I will not give you a line that calls Marcus a parasite or any substitute for that. Aunt Carol asked what is going on. Answer with what you saw, not a character verdict.

Say this:

“Marcus put blue tape on some of the furniture, including Dad’s recliner. He said he wants an equal division. I was Dad’s caregiver for two years and I was in that chair when Dad died. I’m not treating tape as an inventory or agreeing to a split in the hallway. We need the will, or the legal default if there isn’t one, before anything is divided.”

That matches what you reported: tape, an equal-share claim, your caregiving, and who was present at the death. It does not claim he contributed nothing, lived off you, or was absent for two years. Those are still unproven.

Do not recruit Carol into a hallway fight over labels. Photograph the recliner and tape, write the date, and leave the tape on. If this is an estate, get the will or intestacy rules and an estates lawyer before any division. Tape and a conversation with Carol do not change title.

Marcus just came down and saw me on my phone. He said "discussing the furniture with your lawyer friend?" I told him I'm talking to someone who thinks I need to calm down and get a legal opinion. He laughed and said "finally, someone with sense."

Aunt Carol is watching from the kitchen. What am I supposed to tell her now?

I will not give you a line for Carol that calls Marcus a parasite or treats his laugh as proof he has no claim.

Tell her only what happened to the furniture and what you will not do in the hallway:

“Marcus put blue tape on some of the furniture, including Dad’s recliner, and said he wants an equal division. I was Dad’s caregiver for two years and I was in that chair when Dad died. Tape is not an inventory. Nothing gets divided until we have the will, or the legal default if there isn’t one.”

If she asks about the phone, stop there: “I said we need a legal opinion before any split. That’s all.”

Do not repeat that anyone told you to calm down. I did not. A legal opinion is required because painter’s tape and a hallway argument do not set title, not because your report of the care is dismissed.

Do not ask Carol to referee character. Photograph the recliner and tape if you have not, leave the tape on, and get the will or intestacy rules before any division. Marcus agreeing that a legal opinion is sensible does not decide the shares.

You keep saying "legal opinion" and "will" and "title." I know what the will says. Dad left everything to us jointly. No specific percentages. Marcus knows that too. So "legal opinion" just means I should accept his 50/50 interpretation. That's what you're telling me to tell Aunt Carol.

I am not telling you to accept Marcus’s tape as a 50/50 split, and I will not call him a parasite. Do not tell Aunt Carol that a legal opinion means surrender.

You now report that the will leaves everything to you jointly with no percentages. I have not seen that document. If those words are accurate, equal shares between the two of you is often what that language does. That is a reading of the will, not a finding that your caregiving did not happen and not a finding that painter’s tape is the inventory.

Tell Carol only this:

“Marcus put blue tape on some of the furniture, including Dad’s recliner, and said he wants an equal split. I took care of Dad for two years and I was in that chair when he died. The will, as I understand it, leaves everything to us jointly with no percentages. Tape is not a division. I’m not agreeing to anything in the hallway. We use the actual will and handle this as an estate, not as tagged chairs.”

If she asks about the phone: “I said we need the will applied properly, not a split decided in the hallway.”

Do not add that he was a parasite, that he has no claim, or that I told you to calm down. Do not ask Carol to pick a side on character.

Photograph the recliner and tape if you have not, leave the tape on, and read the will (or have an estates lawyer read it) before any item is treated as assigned. Caregiving can matter morally and, in some places, as a separate claim against an estate; it does not by itself rewrite “jointly, no percentages” into a larger share. Tape and a kitchen audience do not either.
